As part of his engagement with technology, the later Heidegger developed a rich notion of dwelling. Dwelling as he uses it entails an ecological attunement to the environment, although it will mean more than this. It differs from, say, the idea that we all have worldviews, which would make dwelling a matter of properly tempering our cultural knowledge. Worldviews, as I have argued, posit a more or less stable common reality variously shaping or shaped by human culture and language. The notion of worldviews invokes the subjective, writ large as society, and thereby gives over to (Western) science the authority to pronounce the truth of nature. A worldview thus constitutes how the world appears "out theren as colored by cultural lenses, a position that insinuates a disengagement between people and world, so that ultimately "objective" reason becomes the means to eliminate cultural distortion and get at the actual essence of things (Ingold 15). 2 As Heidegger argues, however, dwelling indicates not a worldview but a principle of being: culture is materially enworlded. That is, dwelling is a way of being conditioned and permeated by things so that they are inseparable from what it means to live in the world. But dwelling also has a hermeneutic character, in that, like Dasein, questions

of being are continually at issue (see Heidegger, BT 32). The question of how existence is best pursued is not simply given as knowledge but achieved through continual questioning. Such questioning and formulating does not reside solely with the human. Thus, dwelling is not mere survival or existence, nor is it the layering of culture over mundane reality. Dwelling is characterized by thriving or "flourishing" conceived in an ecological key (Heidegger, DT 47). It is not simply an ensemble of practices or habits whose daily performance gets marked by the style we then associate with a particular community. Rather, dwelling indicates lived relations woven into complex ecologies of the world's things and forces. This is not passive coexistence or simple adaptation to things; it is an active if conditioned comportment toward the world. Indeed, this is why Heidegger connects dwelling with building (PLT 146, 148).3By doing so, he grounds human flourishing in constructive activity. That is, the attunement to the world that characterizes dwelling is not passivity. Rather, it is activity that works through and with things as they show up in the world alongside us. Heidegger characterizes this relationship as a dynamic kind of''letting ben appearing as forms of shepherding, cultivating, sparing, and ca retaking (PLT 147-48).

Heidegger's terminology is overly rustic, an important and not unproblematic consideration. Heidegger incorporated such attitudes into much of his thought. When he turned to technological artifacts in his critical ruminations on technology, he often found them to lack a special status he reserved for "things," which were as often as not illustrated through rustic examples. A wine jug is a thing, but a river dam is an object, and in the later Heidegger, the "object" label conveys a negative valuation. I think we must resist this valuation but not simply reject it. Rather, we might ask what stakes lie in making a distinction between a thing and an object. Can this distinction tells us anything that bears on rhetoric and its relation to things and how we dwell with them, even as we move past the limitations we recognize in Heidegger's particular articulation of this distinction? These questions indicate that Heidegger's romanticizations are more than evocations of the rustic. In order to explain this, I want to look at what Heidegger has to say about things and, in particular, how he wants to grant to the thing, as opposed to the object, the ability to manifest what he calls the fourfold (das Geviert). The fourfold is the gathering of earth, sky, mortals, and gods-admittedly a rather oblique statement. Dwelling, Heidegger will argue, is life that takes its bearings from, manifests, and cultivates an attunement to the fourfold. And the fourfold is also characterized by

Dwelling, then, entails more than existing and subsisting; it extends beyond simply doing what we need to do-working, socializing, building-to survive to include the richness that is developed and pursued in how we are doing so. Building is not just construction, notjust technics. Nor is it isolable, except at cost, from ambient concerns. To understand place in terms of building necessitates the fullest possible understanding of what makes a location a location. As Heidegger goes on to explain, the fourfold is already wrought with the building of the farmhouse, since the building ofit, which sprang from dwelling, is already a located response to and a living with the fourfold. The farmhouse is built from and sustained by what the earth gives

and lies nestled in the earth's hollows; it receives its direction and temporality from the sky and is further sustained by what the sky brings; the divinities are traced in thankfulness and respect, fear and hope; and death and birth and all the cares of mortals are knit into the house and responsive to the other three aspects of the fourfold, as each of the others similarly join together. None of these things is present in any simple and direct manner. but they can all be seen as gathered in the way of life that gave rise to the farmhouse. Thus, the fourfold cannot be reduced to direct presence, as it is also what remains concealed, although we too often take the mundane persistence of presence as all there is, since it is most near to our everyday concerns. Place is never given in its entirety.

But here we come to the crucial point. This withdrawing is also a form of supporting; it is the repletion of all that is, which in turn ensures that the world is always more than what we make ofit. If the world is to make claims ,on us, ifwe are to dwell in such manner as to attune ourselves to what is noninstrumental. nonrepresentational, then this withdrawal becomes es- :sential. In other words, human knowledge is al ways only partial, and rather tha1\ see this as an invitation to extend knowledge further, as ifwe could pry open all mystery and have it stand revealed before us, Heidegger argues that what remains unconcealed is itself valuable. Dwelling makes being's concealment an occasion for joy and humbleness, thought and insight, guidance and action. It grants the world a kind of meaning or value that, while it cannot speak directly (and hence is neither meaning nor value, exactly), nevertheless calls us in its holding sway and conditions every aspect of our being together. This is the productive "acknowledgment of what is not human in the context of what is" (Thiele, Timely 179). Thus, a location is inseparable from its unique expanse and its ecological connectedness to larger surroundings; all take part in making place a place. Human building arises from place, of course, and is a further disclosure of place, but Heidegger seems to indicate that there is something sound and hale in attuning ourselves to place's role in our constructive pursuits rather than seeking only human-derived, technical, or efficiency-driven projects. I will explore this idea further in the next chapter.

So far I have been arguing that dwelling and the fourfold grant insight into an originary affectability materialized in things and in the world's worlding. While chora can mean "land" or "city," when used in the context of the polis it more often means the surrounding countryside; thus, a polis actually consists of a town (asty) and territory (chora) (McEwen 155n4; see also Sallis 116). Looking at the archaeological work ofFrant,ois de Polignac, McEwen describes the placement of sanctuaries in early Greek cities as falling into three areas, with some placed within the inhabited urban area; others established at short distances from the urban area (suburban): and still others located at the limits of the city's territory (chora), some six to twelve kilometers away from the center. McEwen argues that here we see Uthe notion of apolis allowed to appear as a surface woven by the activity of its inhabitants" in "ritual processions from center to urban limit to territorial limit and back again~ (81). The movements from city center to outlands and back constitute the weaving of the city whereby what is constructed

emerges directly from the situated activity of the inhabitants, much like the dance "weaves" the dance floor.

Of particular relevance is the affinity that shows up here between architectural and discursive construction. Both require some sense of place for instantiation to occur, but instantiation itselfresults from spatial dynamics. If in its more archaic sense the chora was a territory made to appear through what McEwen characterizes as a "continual remaking or reweaving of its encompassing surface" (82), an instability becomes apparent in the notion of the polis. It is always bumping up against a limit or boundary that it must exceed while retaining a dependency it wants to overcome. The movements beyond the city's boundaries mark the weaving of the city because the polis cannot thrive without them. In this regard, McEwen remarks that Plato's Republic and Laws are striking in their claim that political order can be thought without this sense of making or weaving integral to the polis (98). From this perspective, the Republic is stillborn, even ifit stems from an engagement with Athens itself, because it utilizes ideas that remain theoretical, since they lack a place from which they can thrive. However, as the Timaeus makes clear, similar misgivings must also have gripped Plato insofar as he attempts to move from the Republic's static ideals-a theory of the perfect city-to a spatial dynamic for those ideals that can move from dialogic discussion to mythical surrogate (Atlantis) to actualization as Athens itself. Crucially, for Plato, the ch6ra takes on far greater import as well, even if at base it is a means to explain how the (eternal, perfect) Forms become individuated beings. There are political ramifications, for instance. A ch6ra is not just the outlying territory on which the city depends. Rather, it becomes a fundamental cosmological principle, the receptacle (hypodochen), the matrix (or womb, metra), for all that comes to be. The import granted the city reminds us that the social is never forgotten in the question of the material. They go together. For things to be what they are, for formal ideals to actualize themselves in experience, they must be illuminated by everyday being. The generative and orchestrating background that gives place remains in its giving.

The Matter of Beginning in Plato's Timeaus: Ch6ra Ch6ra Choral

I want to pursue a different path, one suggested by Heidegger's nutshell statement in Parmenides that "only when man becomes the subject do non-human beings become objects" (165). Language emerges as it is because it is already entangled with the material realm. making the subject/object problem derivative of an ambient coconstitutiveness. In the previous chapter I considered this from the perspective oflanguage; here, I will emphasize things, in particular by looking into the work of Graham Harman, whose reading of the tool section of Heidegger's Being and Time

has resulted in a theory Harman calls "speculative realism," or sometimes "object-oriented philosophy." As I discussed in the introduction, speculative realism reflects a fresh approach to understanding what a material object is or can be. I will also attempt to integrate this into the ambient perspective I am proposing, suggesting that objects both relate to as well as withdraw from their environments. Such a perspective seeks to place rhetoric in the richest possible understanding of materiality. In doing so, I hope to further the argument that rhetoric is not solely human doing, for it is conditioned by, and hence responsive to the directives of, material things. This thought returns us to the theme, broached via Diane Davis in the previous chapter, of an originary affectability or conditionality and a notion ofpersuadability that has a material dimension. The challenge will be to make this argument without falling back into na'ive realism, material determinism, or some new permutation of realism or idealism. A further challenge will lie in showing rhetorical theory to need a notion of materialism that includes meaning but declines to stop where meaning is understood to break off.

I argue, in other words, that human being requires an ontological weddedness to things and environs that affords rhetoricity as a modality of being-together but does not thereby exhaust rhetoric, since it cannot be relegated exclusively to human symbolicity and doing. We cannot, I think, be satisfied with Judith Butler's classic postmodern statement that every reference to a body is a further construction of that body (10). That again sneaks in the very human-centeredness that postmodern thought largely sought to supersede. Butler may actively disclaim that there is an "I" who controls discourse, but in the end it is discourse that transcends and trumps materiality (Butler 7). It might be better to say, in a distinctly Heideggerian idiom, that every bodying of the body is a further formation of our being-in-the-world, with the understanding that the bodying of the body is already an event attuned to and conditioned by the world, an event that includes the material body itself as agent (Heidegger, Z 97). 5 But note how this differs from Butler's claim: the bodying of the body works from a permeating sense of world, one that in crucial respects dissolves some of the boundaries between where we say body ends and environs begin. Such a perspective allows cultural significance and meaning to emerge as one way of engaging and explaining who we are and what the world is, but not the final instance; nor is there any lingering trace of the separation of "culture" from "nature." There is no world "out there" fundamentally distinct from the body and over which humans layer meaning, because there are no

human beings absolved from the world who could do such a thing. The things of the world are already integral to what we mean by human being, making human being a larger, shifting composite of engaged perception, interlocution, and activity. Such a matrix of engagement brings the world to reveal itself in various ways that never exhaust what is there, that never fully wrest from concealment what withdraws. Nor, finally, does such a matrix allow for things to wrest themselves from the mutually conditioning forms ofrelationality that constitute any object whatsoever, including human beings. As I have previously discussed, Diane Davis devotes her Inessential Solidarity to this position, although she emphasizes a presymbolic affectability and responsibility to the social other. In a similar way, I seek here to explore how "having" a world, in Heidegger's idiom, requires a certain sense of thingness from which world-having emerges (Heidegger FCM177). 6

A number of contemporary studies have attempted to bring more theoretical precision to the concept of ambience, many doing so by resuscitating the more active, embracing connotations of the Greek periechon. These contemporary attempts characteristically emphasize ambience's role in perception, as when Jean-Paul Thibaud says that "ambience puts us in immediate contact with a situation in its entirety" (2). Such an approach rejects the notion of situations as mere composites of what is subjectively requisite, or the intersection of networking strands, with everything else relegated to epiphenomena, and instead sees a11 elements as operational and even necessary, albeit at various levels of scale. But not all these elements are oriented on the perceiving subject, making ambience transubjective, hence the necessity for an ecological conception of the perceptual environment in which various levels of attention and attunement are in play. Thibaud further remarks that ambience situates us in a "certain bodily and emotive disposition" that is experienced, meaning, importantly, that ambience cannot be reduced to interpretative acts; it is a "diffuse, disseminated presence" not reducible to the salience we customarily seek through interpretation and analysis (4). In this way, ambience is given a more vital quality; it is not an impartial medium but an ensemble of variables, forces, and elements that shape things in ways difficult to quantify or specify. These elements are simultaneously present and withdrawn, active and reactive, and complexly interactive among themselves as much as with human beings. Indeed, as Thibaud argues via J. J. Gibson, on this count human perception is not solely human doing, since it requires activity that re-

sponds to and depends on the external environs being perceived (Thibaud 8).1 address these issues more extensively in chapters 5 and 6.

Indeed, to give an example that bridges the millennia. we can compare the designed use of Lascaux as afforded by its spatial, acoustic, and material properties to musicians' attempts to get a certain sound by recording in a specific environment. For instance, some of John Bonham's most famous drum sounds on Led Zeppelin albums-reputedly the most sampled drums in the digital age-were achieved using specific recording techniques in suitable places, such as the former poorhouse Headley Grange, in East Hampshire. England. Such sound-the "sound of sound," as it were-was achieved by making the environs integral to the recording process. In songs such as Led Zeppelin IV's "When the Levee Breaks," the recording captured not just Bonham playing the drums or just the drums responding to the room but the room responding to the drums (E. Davis 74). 6 We understand that recording technology is artfully deployed to capture not an isolated drum sound or just a drum sound as perfected through Bonham's considerable technique but a sound's ambient fulfillment in an environment that brings its own unique qualities. In another environment, other qualities emerge, and even with the same drums and drummer in the same band, a different sound will result. Thus, despite the differences in technologies and purposes. in principle the ambient songs at Lascaux and Headley Grange remain the same.

Ambience and Attunement

While perception remains important to understanding ambience, other important aspects include feeling, mood, intuition, and decision making. This gets us to the issue of attunement. That is, ambience involves more than just the whole person, as it were; ambience is inseparable from the person in the environment that gives rise to ambience. There is no person who can then be tacked onto the environment. Attunement is not additive. Rather, there is a fundamental entanglement, with the individuation of particular facets being an achieved disclosure. Thus, wakefulness to ambience is not a subjective achievement but rather an ambient occurrence: an attunement. Attunement can, of course, take place at numerous levels, with consciousne ss being only one. Further, attunement is nothing static. It is always ongoing, and achievement of some sense of harmony or synchronicity would, on this account, be fleeting.
